title: Dakota Ridge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dakota Ridge wells have a 130 ft median depth, but local records range widely. See yields, water levels, costs and risks before buying.
intro_html:
Buying land in Dakota Ridge means treating the well as part of the property, not as a guaranteed utility. Records within five miles show 2,366 permitted wells, with 1,300 recorded as constructed. Reported conditions vary widely across this mountain area, particularly where fractured bedrock and Denver Basin formations affect drilling.

The local median well is 130 feet deep, and the median reported pump yield is 10.0 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not predict one specific lot. Review the permit, well construction, water-rights limitations, neighboring wells and site conditions before closing or starting construction.

sections.heading: Dakota Ridge well depths vary sharply by ground
sections.html:
The median reported depth near Dakota Ridge is 130 feet. The middle half of reported wells runs from 35 to 405 feet, so a driller bidding a new well should not treat 130 feet as a firm target. It is a starting point for estimating, not a guarantee.

About 45% of wells are under 100 feet, while 20% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 22% between 300 and 600 feet, and 13% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 4,095 feet. Permits commonly identify unnamed fractured bedrock, with Denver Basin aquifer wells making up 68% of the records. Rock structure, the selected aquifer and the lot’s position can drive the final depth.

sections.heading: What Dakota Ridge wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 250 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 5.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute, which is a workable planning range for many household systems when the storage and pump equipment are properly sized.

Reported results are not evenly distributed. 59% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, 22% report more than 15, 17% fall between 1 and 5, and 2% are under 1 gallon per minute. A low-yield well may still work with storage, but it deserves a specific design review. Ask for the well test, permitted use and recovery information rather than relying on a neighbor’s result.

sections.heading: Water levels near Ken Caryl and Morrison
sections.html:
Only 57 wells report a static water level, so the water-level data is thinner than the depth data. In that group, the median depth to water is 33 feet**, with the middle half from 18 to 150 feet. That spread matters when estimating pump setting, trenching and the risk of encountering water at different elevations.

The median reported level was 30 feet below surface in the 2010s and 25 feet in the 2020s. That does not show a dropping water table in this record set; the later median is shallower. The limited sample and changing measurement locations make it unsuitable for predicting a particular parcel. Confirm conditions with a current well test and nearby permits in Dakota Ridge, Ken Caryl and Morrison.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Dakota Ridge
sections.html:
Well activity has continued across the area. The records show 68 permits from the 1950s, 75 from the 1960s, 237 from the 1970s, 205 from the 1980s, 362 from the 1990s, 358 from the 2000s, 160 from the 2010s and 233 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

In the records, the most active listed driller is Authorized (Pe, Pg), associated with 531 wells. Hier Drilling Co Inc, listed as Hier, Bruce A., appears on 74, and James Drilling Company, listed as Keaton, Michael K., on 56. These are record patterns, not endorsements or proof of current availability.

sections.heading: Planning a new well budget in Dakota Ridge
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 130-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone works out to about $6,500 to $9,100. That is not the full project price.

A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $12,500 to $21,100. A bid should state what happens if the hole must go deeper, the yield is poor, casing or grout requirements change, or access requires extra excavation. Compare bids by scope, not just by the per-foot number. Include well permitting, water testing and any storage or treatment equipment that the proposed household system may need.

sections.heading: Risks to investigate before you buy or build
sections.html:
Environmental screening deserves attention around Dakota Ridge. Within about ten miles, the map includes 241 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 91 historic mine features and 78 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site does not establish contamination on a specific parcel, but it is a reason to order a current laboratory water test and review the site history.

Low yield, a dry hole and fractured-rock variability are separate risks from water quality. Check the permitted use, construction record, casing and grout, pump test and static level. Confirm that the proposed house, septic system, driveway and reserve area fit the lot. Domestic wells are subject to Colorado water-rights rules; an exempt household-use well is not a guarantee of unrestricted irrigation or additional dwelling use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dakota Ridge, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Dakota Ridge is 130 feet. The middle half ranges from 35 to 405 feet, while 13% of records are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record is 4,095 feet. Local fractured bedrock and Denver Basin conditions make a parcel-specific estimate more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Dakota Ridge?
faq.a: Among 250 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 5.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. About 2% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 17% report 1 to 5. Ask for a current well test and consider storage if the yield is low.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Dakota Ridge?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 130-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $6,500 to $9,100. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $12,500 to $21,100. Actual bids can change if the hole must go deeper or access and construction requirements differ.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Dakota Ridge?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a regional median. Within about ten miles, records map 241 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 91 historic mine features and 78 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a parcel is affected. Order a current laboratory test and review nearby land uses, mine history and well construction.

faq.q: Should I test a Dakota Ridge well before buying?
faq.a: Yes. The records show wide variation in depth, yield and static water level, and only 57 wells report static levels. Request the permit and construction record, pump test, water-quality results and service history. Compare nearby wells in Dakota Ridge, Ken Caryl, Morrison, Columbine and Bow Mar, but use those records as context rather than a substitute for testing the property.
